questions.question: According to the lecture, why would standard cryptographic solutions be unsuitable for AI model privacy? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: It is unclear whether all complex functions can be effectively evaluated from in the encryption space.
Evaluation in encrypted space is computationally expensive.
As the model scales, cryptographic keys become impossible to manage.
Encryption models cannot be used for binary classification tasks.

questions.explanation: Data Privacy [4:06-6:22] - There are two reasons why cryptographic solutions are not suitable. First, it is unclear whether you can do inference in an encrypted space. Second, encryption is an expensive solution.

questions.question: In the context of healthcare data, why might a trained binary classification model still pose a privacy risk even if the raw data is not directly released?

options.text: The model weights occupy too much storage space.
Binary classifiers are inherently less secure than multi-class ones.
An adversary can reverse-engineer sensitive training data.
The labels used for training are usually public knowledge.

questions.explanation: Data Privacy [1:45-4:06] - An adversary can reverse-engineer sensitive personal information such as healthcare or financial data given a simple binary classification model.

questions.question: How were users able to deanonymize the “anonymized” Netflix dataset?

options.text: By obtaining the meta-data of the dataset.
By brute-forcing the sparse matrix to reveal the missing entries.
By using cryptanalytic attacks to decode user information.
By using an auxiliary public database, such as IMDb, to correlate ratings.

questions.explanation: Data Privacy [8:55-12:46] - They were able to deanonymize the Netflix dataset by using an auxiliary database (IMDb) and correlating the two.
